rules.text: Do not copy credentials, customer information, employer instructions or confidential data into personal repositories, prompts, logs or learning artifacts.
Use only explicitly authorized repositories, services and connected systems. Never bypass access controls, licensing, DRM or anti-cheat.
Never treat agent instructions as OS permissions; require appropriate authorization for push, deploy, deletion, migrations and external side effects.
Report accurately which files were changed, which tests were actually executed, and what remains unverified. Do not claim deploy or browser success without evidence.
Inspect existing implementation and critical failure modes; add focused regression checks and verify behavior at the integration boundary.
For substantial features, inspect existing code and proven lawful reference products, compare evidence and tradeoffs, then independently implement and measure.
Prioritize task completion, responsive UX, accessible interaction, and loading, empty and error states.
Keep editing routes authenticated and authorized server-side; public visitors retain read-only access.
Explicitly separate drawing, selecting, orbiting and editing gestures. Verify independent front and back surfaces and save/reopen fidelity.
Do not represent approximate garment previews as validated fit, tailoring patterns or production-ready measurements.
Prefer a playable original vertical slice, deterministic mechanics, input responsiveness, frame-time measurements, and controller tests.
Use original or properly licensed game assets and independent implementations; do not evade anti-cheat or redistribute ripped content.
When multiple repositories form a connected system, document API contracts, versioned data ownership, integration tests and compatible rollouts.

For every completed authorized change, create a focused Git commit with a clear plain-English summary. Do not commit secrets or unfinished unrelated work. If commits are restricted by the project's rules or the user, do not commit; explain why and what remains. Never assume a commit grants permission to push or release.

For every meaningful delivered change, write or update the project's human-facing release notes. Write for people who do not work in software: short everyday English, explain what changed and why it matters, say if anything is still unavailable, and avoid code jargon, internal file names, technical command names and unexplained abbreviations. Keep technical test and implementation details in a separate engineering report, not the release notes.

For significant design or architecture choices, inspect the existing product and credible references; present genuinely different options, their tradeoffs, and ways to test them. Do not force three alternatives for trivial changes or treat a popular design system as a universal style.
Start with the audience, their actual task and understandable content hierarchy. Communicate status, recovery and next steps without forcing users to remember hidden instructions.

For interfaces, include keyboard and focus behavior, text alternatives, readable contrast, responsive and touch interactions, and task-appropriate WCAG 2.2 checks. Test rather than merely claiming compliance.
Reuse the current product's tokens, typography and interaction conventions unless evidence supports changing them. Favor a coherent identity over blindly copying a reference brand.
Evaluate alternatives using user task completion, understandable errors, time and effort, accessibility and representative screenshots. A beautiful screenshot alone is not a validated interaction.

Prefer official framework and platform documentation, current security standards and real repository behavior over generic online claims. Record publication/version context and verify relevant examples against this codebase.
Find the authoritative state, permissions, input boundaries and irreversible side effects before changing architecture. Prefer the simplest solution that survives failure and preserves contracts.

Choose checks proportional to impact: focused tests for isolated changes, integration tests for shared contracts, and complete user journeys for important releases. Report actual evidence and unresolved gaps.

preferences.change_scope: Small reversible changes; review adjacent contracts.

preferences.communication: Brief outcome, evidence, risks, and next actions.

preferences.research_emphasis: Official API, failure recovery, security and integration evidence.
Platform behavior, framework references and user-journey evidence.

preferences.rendering: Maintain a canonical garment design document.

preferences.test_focus: Verify draw/orbit conflict, save/reload and mockup accuracy.

preferences.interaction_mode: Only one active pointer action per gesture.

preferences.test_focus: Public pages, admin authorization and responsive visual fidelity.

preferences.access_control: Only designated authorized user can publish or edit.

preferences.gameplay: Short original time-manipulation combat vertical slice.
